questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If I have more money, I would travel around the world.
If I had more money, I would travel around the world.
If I had more money, I will travel around the world.
If I would have more money, I would travel around the world.
questions.explanation: Second conditional: If + past simple, would + base verb: 'If I had more money, I would travel around the world.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: If she had left earlier, she wouldn't miss the flight.
If she left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the flight.
If she had left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the flight.
If she would have left earlier, she wouldn't have missed the flight.
questions.explanation: Third conditional: If + past perfect, would have + past participle: 'If she had left..., she wouldn't have missed...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: This airport uses by thousands of passengers every day.
This airport is using by thousands of passengers every day.
This airport use by thousands of passengers every day.
This airport is used by thousands of passengers every day.
questions.explanation: Present simple passive: is/are + past participle: 'is used by thousands of passengers.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The flight delayed because of bad weather.
The flight was delayed because of bad weather.
The flight was delay because of bad weather.
The flight is delayed because of bad weather.
questions.explanation: Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: 'was delayed because of bad weather.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The guide who showed us the museum was very knowledgeable.
The guide which showed us the museum was very knowledgeable.
The guide whom showed us the museum was very knowledgeable.
The guide, who showed us the museum, was very knowledgeable but.
questions.explanation: 'Who' introduces a defining relative clause about a person: 'The guide who showed us the museum...'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Our hotel which overlooks the sea is fully booked in summer but.
Our hotel which overlooks the sea, is fully booked in summer.
Our hotel, which overlooks the sea, is fully booked in summer.
Our hotel, that overlooks the sea, is fully booked in summer.
questions.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses use commas and 'which' for things: 'Our hotel, which overlooks the sea, is fully booked.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That can't be our gate, the sign says something else.
That can't to be our gate, the sign says something else.
That can't being our gate, the sign says something else.
That cann't be our gate, the sign says something else.
questions.explanation: 'Can't' + base verb expresses a confident negative deduction: 'that can't be our gate.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: The plane could being delayed because of the storm.
The plane could be delayed because of the storm.
The plane could to be delayed because of the storm.
The plane coulds be delayed because of the storm.
questions.explanation: 'Could' + base verb expresses a possible deduction: 'the plane could be delayed.'

questions.topic: Present perfect vs present perfect continuous
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've visited six countries this year.
I've been visiting six countries this year.
I've visit six countries this year.
I'm visiting six countries this year already.
questions.explanation: Present perfect simple is used for a completed number of results: 'I've visited six countries.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I've travelled around Europe since two months.
I'm travelling around Europe for two months already.
I've been travel around Europe for two months.
I've been travelling around Europe for two months.
questions.explanation: Present perfect continuous emphasizes duration of an unfinished action: 'I've been travelling... for two months.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "I have booked the hotel.")
options: She said that she has booked the hotel.
She said that she had booked the hotel.
She said that she booked the hotel already.
She said she have booked the hotel.
questions.explanation: In reported speech, present perfect shifts back to past perfect: 'she had booked the hotel.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence. (Direct: "Which airline do you prefer?")
options: He asked me which airline do I prefer.
He asked me which airline did I prefer.
He asked me which airline I preferred.
He asked me which airline I prefer.
questions.explanation: Reported questions use normal word order (no auxiliary inversion) and shift the tense back: 'he asked me which airline I preferred.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I used to travel by train every summer as a child.
I use to travel by train every summer as a child.
I was used to travel by train every summer as a child.
I used to travelling by train every summer as a child.
questions.explanation: 'Used to' + base verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'I used to travel by train every summer.'

questions.topic: Be used to / get used to
questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I'm used to drive on the left now.
I'm used to driving on the left now.
I use to driving on the left now.
I'm used driving to the left now.
questions.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund: 'I'm used to driving on the left.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We set off for the airport at dawn.
We set the airport off at dawn.
We set for off the airport at dawn.
We set the airport at dawn off.
questions.explanation: 'Set off' means 'start a journey': 'set off for the airport.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Passengers must check the flight in two hours before departure.
Passengers must check in to two hours before departure.
Passengers must check two hours in before departure.
Passengers must check in two hours before departure.
questions.explanation: 'Check in' means 'register for a flight/hotel': 'check in two hours before departure.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Despite the delay, we arrived on time.
Despite of the delay, we arrived on time.
Although the delay, we arrived on time.
Despite the delay was long, we arrived on time.
questions.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase (no 'of'): 'Despite the delay, we arrived on time.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: He forgot his passport. As a result, he missed the flight.
He forgot his passport, as a result he missed the flight.
As a result he forgot his passport he missed the flight.
He forgot his passport as a result, he missed the flight.
questions.explanation: 'As a result' starts a new sentence and is followed by a comma: 'He forgot his passport. As a result, he missed the flight.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: We don't have enough time to see the whole city.
We don't have time enough to see the whole city.
We don't have enough of time to see the whole city.
We hasn't enough time to see the whole city.
questions.explanation: 'Enough' comes before the noun it modifies: 'enough time.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: My sister is really interested in backpacking.
My sister is really interested at backpacking.
My sister is really interested for backpacking.
My sister is really interested to backpacking.
questions.explanation: 'Interested in' + noun/gerund means 'curious/enthusiastic about': 'interested in backpacking.'

questions.question: Which is the correct way to start an email to a hotel you haven't stayed at, asking about availability?
options: Hey there,
Dear Sir or Madam,
Yo,
What's up,
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir or Madam,' is a suitable formal opening when the recipient's exact name is unknown.

questions.question: Which is the correct way to end a formal email to a named hotel manager?
options: Yours faithfully,
Best regards,
Later,
Cheers mate,
questions.explanation: 'Best regards,' is a suitable semi-formal closing when writing to a named professional contact.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I was wondering if you could confirm my reservation.
I was wondering if you could to confirm my reservation.
I was wondering could you confirming my reservation.
I wonder if you confirm could my reservation.
questions.explanation: 'I was wondering if you could' + base verb is a polite way to make a request: 'if you could confirm my reservation.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly combines 'This is the tourist.' and 'The tourist's luggage was lost.'?
options: This is the tourist whose luggage was lost.
This is the tourist who luggage was lost.
This is the tourist which luggage was lost.
This is the tourist's luggage who was lost.
questions.explanation: 'Whose' shows possession in a relative clause: 'the tourist whose luggage was lost.'

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I have never seen such a beautiful beach before.
I have seen never such a beautiful beach before.
Never I have seen such a beautiful beach before.
I have seen such a beautiful beach never before.
questions.explanation: 'Never' is placed between the auxiliary and the past participle: 'I have never seen such a beach.'

questions.question: Which sentence has correct punctuation?
options: I'd like to know whether the train has been cancelled.
I'd like to know whether has the train been cancelled?
I'd like to know, whether the train has been cancelled.
I'd like to know whether the train has been cancelled?
questions.explanation: Reported/indirect statements use normal word order and end with a full stop, not a question mark.

questions.question: This time tomorrow, I ___ on a plane to Rome.
options: will fly
will be flying
am flying
fly
questions.explanation: Future continuous describes an action in progress at a specific future time: 'will be flying'.

questions.question: By next month, they ___ five countries.
options: will visit
will have visited
visit
are visiting
questions.explanation: Future perfect describes an action completed before a future point: 'will have visited'.

questions.question: Choose the sentence that correctly uses discourse markers.
options: Firstly, pack your bags. Secondly, check your passport. Finally, head to the airport.
Firstly we pack bags secondly check finally airport.
Finally pack the bags, firstly check, secondly head airport.
Secondly firstly pack bags, finally check passport.
questions.explanation: Discourse markers 'Firstly,', 'Secondly,' and 'Finally,' organize points clearly with commas.

questions.question: Choose the correct question tag.
options: You wouldn't forget your passport, would you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, do you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, wouldn't you?
You wouldn't forget your passport, will you?
questions.explanation: Negative statement with 'would' + positive tag: 'you wouldn't forget..., would you?'
